say: You give it a data set and a percentage. It finds the value that has that percentage of the data **below** it.
The $80$th percentile is the score with $80\%$ of the scores under it, so you find its position by taking that percentage of the number of scores.

example.question:
Twenty students sat a test. Their scores, in order, were:
$34, 41, 45, 48, 52, 55, 57, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70, 71, 73, 75, 78, 82, 85, 91$
Find the $80$th percentile score.

steps.title: Count how many are below
steps.say: The $80$th percentile has $80\%$ of the scores below it. Find $80\%$ of the $20$ scores.

lines.text: So $16$ scores lie below the percentile.

steps.title: Find the cut-off place
steps.say: With $\hl{1}{16}$ scores below, the cut-off is between the $16$th and $17$th scores in the ordered list.

steps.title: Take the midpoint
steps.say: The cut-off falls exactly between two scores, so take the value halfway between them.

say: You give it a description of how a study chose its people. It names the method (**stratified**, cluster or quota), and says what bias or control it needs.
The key idea is who gets picked. Stratified splits the group into types and samples each type in proportion. Cluster picks whole groups. Quota fills set numbers but not at random.

how.higher: It came up once, in 2025 Paper 2 Q10(d), for 5 marks: describe how to take a stratified random sample and say why one grouping would not be useful.

example.question: A school has $900$ students: $270$ in 1st year, $225$ in 2nd, $180$ in 3rd, $135$ in 4th and $90$ in 5th. A survey needs a stratified random sample of $60$ students, by year group. Name the method and find how many 3rd years are chosen.

steps.title: Name the method
steps.say: The students are split into year groups and each group is sampled in proportion to its size. That is **stratified** sampling.

lines.text: Each year group is a stratum. Inside each stratum, students must be chosen at random.

steps.title: Find the fraction
steps.say: Each group gets the same fraction of its students. Divide the sample size by the whole school.

steps.title: Apply it to 3rd year
steps.say: Take that fraction of the $180$ third-year students.

lines.text: Choose these $12$ at random from the 3rd years, for example by numbering them and using a random number generator.

higher.tip: When you describe a stratified sample, say the selection within each group is random. It costs a mark if you leave it out.
If asked why a grouping is not useful, say there is probably no link between that grouping and the thing being measured.

sources.quote: Probably no connection between owning a pet

say: You give it pairs of values, $x$ and $y$. The calculator returns $r$, the **correlation coefficient**.
$r$ lies between $-1$ and $1$. Near $1$ the points rise along a line, near $-1$ they fall along a line, near $0$ there is no straight-line link.

how.higher: It is the main skill in 4 parts since 2017, always on Paper 2: a part worth 5 to 15 marks that asks for $r$ to a set number of decimal places, often with a comment on what it shows.

example.question:
Five students recorded hours of revision $x$ and test mark $y$:
$(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 7), (5, 9)$.
Find the correlation coefficient $r$, correct to $3$ decimal places, and say what it shows.

steps.title: Enter the data
steps.say: Put the calculator in statistics mode with two variables. Type the $x$ values in one column and the $y$ values in the other.

lines.text: Check each column has $5$ entries before going on.

steps.title: Read off r
steps.say: Ask the calculator for $\hl{1}{r}$. Do not round until the end.

steps.title: Round and interpret
steps.say: Round to $3$ decimal places as asked, then say what the sign and size mean.

lines.text: $r$ is close to $1$: strong positive correlation. More revision goes with higher marks.

higher.tip: Give $r$ to exactly the decimal places asked. A different number of places loses a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * for incorrect rounding in (c)
One or more answers not to

higher.tip: A correct value for $r$ is accepted without working, so use the calculator and write the value down clearly.
If asked why $r$ can mislead, say correlation measures linear relationships and the data follow a curve.

say: You give it a scatter plot. You draw a straight line through the middle of the points, find its equation, and use it to predict.
The key idea is balance. The line follows the trend with points on both sides of it, and you predict by reading or substituting a value of $x$.

how.higher: It appears as part of larger Paper 2 statistics questions, in 2017 and 2022: plot points, draw a reasonable line, then use it to read values.

example.question:
The table shows hours of study $x$ and test mark $y$ for eight students.
$(1, 13), (2, 17), (3, 19), (4, 25), (5, 27), (6, 31), (7, 37), (8, 39)$
A line of best fit drawn by eye passes through $(2, 16)$ and $(8, 40)$. Find its equation and use it to predict the mark for a student who studies for $6$ hours.

steps.title: Draw the line
steps.say: Plot the points. Draw a ruler line through the middle of them with points on both sides, passing through the two given points.

lines.text: The line should follow the trend, not join the first and last point.

steps.title: Find the slope
steps.say: Use the two points on the line to find its $\hl{1}{\text{slope}}$.

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.say: Put the slope and the point $(2, 16)$ into $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.

steps.title: Predict
steps.say: Substitute $x = 6$ into the equation. $6$ is inside the data, so the prediction is reliable.

higher.tip: Draw the line with some points on each side of it and a sensible slope. That is what earns the mark.

sources.quote: accept line of best fit with some

higher.tip: Label the plotted points and show your working on the graph. Without it you lose a mark.
When asked which prediction is less reliable, pick the point far beyond the data. Extrapolating is the weak one.

sources.quote: L is well beyond all of the given data
